findings.title: Public `findMany()` removed without updating any callers
findings.body: `InsightsBookingService.findMany(findManyArgs: Prisma.BookingTimeStatusDenormalizedFindManyArgs)` was deleted and replaced by `getBaseConditions(): Promise<Prisma.Sql>`. This is a breaking change to the service's public surface: any consumer that previously did `service.findMany({ select: ... })` (the old integration test did exactly that) will now fail to compile/run. This PR only touches the service and its test, so if any production code path (insights routers/handlers) calls `findMany`, the build breaks. Either keep a `findMany` wrapper that executes `$queryRaw` with `getBaseConditions()`, or update all call sites in this PR.

findings.title: Public condition getters return unparenthesized composite SQL (operator-precedence hazard)
findings.body: `buildFilterConditions` returns the single-condition case verbatim, e.g. `"eventTypeId" = $1 OR "eventParentId" = $1`, and `buildAuthorizationConditions`/`buildOrgAuthorizationCondition` similarly return top-level `AND`/`OR` expressions with no surrounding parentheses (see also lines 135, 164, 197). `getBaseConditions` happens to wrap them, but these are public async methods (`getAuthorizationConditions`, `getFilterConditions`) and any caller doing `WHERE ${auth} AND ${filters}` or `WHERE ${base} AND "startTime" > $x` will get silently wrong results because `OR` binds looser than `AND` — in the authorization case that means returning bookings the user is not allowed to see. Wrap each produced fragment in parentheses at construction time.

findings.title: New `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions` loses discriminated-union type safety and silently denies access
findings.body: The constructor now accepts `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions` (`scope: "user" | "org" | "team"`, `teamId?: number`) instead of the discriminated union `InsightsBookingServiceOptions`. A caller can now pass `{ scope: "team", userId, orgId }` with no `teamId` and it compiles; at runtime `safeParse` fails, `this.options` becomes `null`, and every query silently returns `1=0` (no rows) with no error or log. Previously this was a compile-time error. Keep the discriminated union in the constructor signature, or at least surface the validation failure (throw/log) instead of degrading to an empty result set.

findings.title: Only user-scope SQL is ever executed against the database; team/org raw SQL is untested
findings.body: The only test that runs real SQL (`$queryRaw ... WHERE ${baseConditions}`) uses `scope: "user"`, which exercises only `"userId"`, `"teamId"`, `"eventTypeId"` and `"eventParentId"`. The team/org conditions, which are the newly hand-written SQL most likely to be wrong (quoted column `"isTeamBooking"`, and `= ANY(${array})` array-parameter binding), are only compared string-wise against hand-copied `Prisma.sql` literals. A misspelled/renamed view column or an array binding the driver rejects would pass all tests and fail in production. Add at least one `$queryRaw` execution for team scope and one for org scope asserting the expected booking ids.

findings.title: Caching tests deleted while the memoization code remains
findings.body: The `describe("Caching")` block covering `cachedAuthConditions`/`cachedFilterConditions` was removed, but the service still memoizes both (`getAuthorizationConditions`/`getFilterConditions`, insightsBooking.ts lines 83-95). The memoization has a subtle contract (`undefined` means "not computed", `null` is a valid cached filter result); with the tests gone, a regression such as recomputing on every call or treating a cached `null` as uncached would go unnoticed. Port the caching assertions to the new `Prisma.sql` expectations instead of dropping them.

findings.title: Org/team scope expectations depend on undefined DB row ordering
findings.body: The expected SQL parameters are arrays in a fixed order (`[org.id, team.id, team2.id, team3.id]` and `[user.id, user2.id, user3.id]`), but these come from `TeamRepository.findAllByParentId` and `MembershipRepository.findAllByTeamIds`, which issue no `ORDER BY`. `toEqual` on arrays is order-sensitive, so this test can fail intermittently depending on Postgres row ordering. Sort the ids before comparing (or compare as sets).
